site.title: Writings
site.author: Suraj Sharma
site.description: Long-form research on agentic systems and the measurement of work.

posts.title: Blink, taken apart
posts.subtitle: Chromium's rendering engine is 213,000 files, and 189,644 of them are web tests. This is a teardown of the rest: how third_party/blink is layered and how that layering is enforced, what runs on which thread, how a byte of HTML and a CSS property name become C++ classes, how one BeginMainFrame becomes pixels, and where Blink hands off to V8, to cc, and to //content. Everything is read at chromium/src@f288fed6 — Chrome 156.0.8067.0, 18 September 2026.

posts.title: DEPS, gclient and what replaced goma
posts.subtitle: Chromium is one git repository plus a 5,188-line file that declares 451 more dependencies across three transports. This is how gclient sync reads that file, how rollers rewrite it about 940 times a week, how the compiler is pinned in text — and how the distributed build underneath went from goma to reclient to Siso.

posts.title: The tree that configures the fleet
posts.subtitle: Chromium's CI is 1,211 builders in 18 buckets, all of them generated by lucicfg from 125 Starlark files inside the repository they build. This is how a change gets from git cl upload to refs/heads/main, how 2.4 million test tasks a day get scheduled, and how a milestone turns into a branch, a version bump and a release.

posts.title: Liveblocks, read for XO Space
posts.subtitle: A reading of the Liveblocks documentation with xo-space in hand: what the product is, where a room-per-project would sit against the watcher and the broker, whether any of it installs inside the container, and what “agents build and share a Space autonomously” would actually mean — with a bounded pilot at the end.

posts.title: The ten hardest open problems in mathematics
posts.subtitle: Ten problems, ranked by how much of mathematics moves when they move: P vs NP, the Riemann hypothesis, Navier–Stokes, Yang–Mills, Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, Hodge, Langlands, twin primes and Goldbach, abc, and Collatz. What each one actually claims, what has actually been proved as of August 2026, and where the frontier now sits — plus the distinction the phrase “NP-hard” usually hides, the places where mathematics is provably NP-hard or undecidable, the four different kinds of infinity and why one of them cannot be measured, and a dated, checkable forecast of which of the ten falls first.

posts.title: XO Space: the architecture
posts.subtitle: The implementation reference for xo-space, the app for understanding and mapping xo-projects. Everything verified against the working tree, stated once, and kept short. This revision adds the full data model: the twelve entities collected across five stores, the field-level session record, what bounds each file as the timeline grows, and a marked proposal for consolidating the plane.

posts.title: The J-Space: a construction manual
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's global-workspace paper reports that a model holds roughly twenty-five concepts at a time in a privileged subspace — under 10% of its activation variance — that it can report on, reason with, and be steered through. The tool that finds it is one averaged Jacobian per layer. A close reading of what a J-space is, then a step-by-step guide to building one: the compute routes, the sparse decomposition, the read and write operations, and the validation protocol.

posts.title: One Graph, No Boxes
posts.subtitle: A close reading of Click and Paleczny's 1995 paper, the origin of the Sea of Nodes — every structural figure redrawn and worked through, from REGION nodes and PHI alignment to memory-as-a-value, the Petri-net execution model, and the experiment whose result surprised its own authors. Then the part that isn't in the paper: the general recipe inside it, and how to apply it to any data you will ever model.

posts.title: The Sea of Nodes, explained simply
posts.subtitle: Compilers usually write your program down as a list of instructions in boxes. V8's TurboFan threw the list away and kept only the dependencies. What that means, the three kinds of edges it needs, why pure instructions float, how the graph becomes a program again — and why V8 eventually sailed back to shore.

posts.title: Anatomy of an Agent Control Plane
posts.subtitle: A component-by-component teardown of xo-space, the local control plane that brokers Claude Code, OpenClaw, Hermes, and Antigravity behind one API: the single capability seam, agents declared as data, four transports under one streaming contract, a session index that deliberately holds no messages, encrypted GitHub-backed snapshots — and why the invariant that keeps agent names out of core is really an instrument.

posts.title: Anatomy of a Personal Memory Engine
posts.subtitle: A component-by-component teardown of iai-pme, a fully local memory engine for coding agents: fail-safe capture hooks, an encrypted verbatim store, a vector index that isn't HNSW, a hyperdimensional substrate, homegrown community detection, nightly consolidation — and what a working Mₜ means for quirq's tenure hypothesis.

posts.title: What is a unit of work?
posts.subtitle: A prompt asks for an action. A unit of work owns an outcome from definition through verification — one owner, a definition of done, a budget, a workspace, a durable result. The quirq is the proposed unit for measuring that verified work.

posts.title: quirq: A Unit of Work for Intelligence
posts.subtitle: AI is metered on one side only. The token counts what the machine consumes; the quirq is proposed as the output meter — value budgeted by an owner, minted by verification against captured world state, costed all-in, and read over time as a trajectory.
